choices.text: A 50 : 50 mixture of two enantiomers
A single compound that has chirality centers but is achiral
choices.why: That is a meso compound. A racemate is a mixture of two different, chiral molecules.

choices.text: A 50 : 50 mixture of two diastereomers
choices.why: Diastereomers rotate light by different amounts, so their rotations wouldn't cancel. A racemate contains the two enantiomers.

choices.text: Any mixture of a chiral compound with an achiral one
choices.why: A racemate contains only the two enantiomers of one chiral compound, in equal amounts.

explanation: A 50 : 50 mixture of the two enantiomers of a chiral compound is called a racemate, or racemic mixture. Pasteur's optically inactive tartaric acid salt was a racemate of the 2R,3R and 2S,3S enantiomers.

prompt: How is a racemic mixture denoted?

choices.text: By the symbol (±) or the prefix d,l
By the prefix meso-
choices.why: meso- names a single achiral compound with chirality centers, such as meso-tartaric acid, not a mixture of enantiomers.

choices.text: By the label R,S
choices.why: Labels like 2R,3S give the configurations of chirality centers within one molecule; they don't describe a mixture.

choices.text: By the symbol (+)
choices.why: (+) marks the dextrorotatory enantiomer alone. A racemate contains both the (+) and (−) forms.

explanation: A racemate is denoted by either the symbol (±) or the prefix d,l to indicate an equal mixture of dextrorotatory and levorotatory forms.

prompt: (+)-Tartaric acid has [α]D = +12. What specific rotation would you observe for racemic (±)-tartaric acid?
explanation: Racemates show no optical rotation because the (+) rotation from one enantiomer exactly cancels the (−) rotation from the other. The +12 of the (+) form is cancelled by the −12 of the (−) form.

prompt: Why does a racemic mixture show no optical rotation?

choices.text: The (+) rotation from one enantiomer exactly cancels the (−) rotation from the other
Its molecules are achiral, because each has a plane of symmetry
choices.why: That explains a meso compound. Each molecule in a racemate is chiral; it is the equal mixture that shows no net rotation.

choices.text: The two enantiomers react with each other to form an achiral compound
choices.why: The enantiomers stay intact in the mixture. Pasteur could even crystallize the two optically active forms out of racemic tartaric acid.

choices.text: Each enantiomer rotates light only weakly
choices.why: Each enantiomer alone is optically active (for tartaric acid, [α]D = +12 or −12). The rotations are equal and opposite, so they cancel.

explanation: A racemate is an equal mixture of dextrorotatory and levorotatory forms. Racemates show no optical rotation because the (+) rotation from one enantiomer exactly cancels the (−) rotation from the other.

prompt: A 12.0 g sample of a racemic mixture contains how many grams of the (+) enantiomer?
explanation: A racemate is a 50 : 50 mixture of the two enantiomers, so half of 12.0 g, 6.0 g, is the (+) enantiomer and 6.0 g is the (−) enantiomer.

prompt: Pasteur crystallized two optically active tartaric acid salts (2R,3R and 2S,3S) from an optically inactive starting salt. Why couldn't that starting material have been meso-tartaric acid?

choices.text: meso-Tartaric acid is a different compound and can't become the chiral enantiomers without breaking and re-forming bonds
meso-Tartaric acid is optically active, so it couldn't have been the inactive starting material
choices.why: meso-Tartaric acid is achiral and optically inactive ([α]D = 0). The problem is that it isn't made of the 2R,3R and 2S,3S molecules.

choices.text: meso-Tartaric acid doesn't form crystals
choices.why: Crystallization isn't the issue. Crystallizing a compound can't turn it into a different compound; meso-tartaric acid would have to break and re-form bonds.

choices.text: It could have been; the meso form is a mixture of the 2R,3R and 2S,3S forms
choices.why: That describes the racemate. The meso form is a single compound, 2R,3S, diastereomeric with the 2R,3R and 2S,3S forms.

explanation: It couldn't have been meso-tartaric acid, because meso-tartaric acid is a different chemical compound and can't interconvert with the two chiral enantiomers without breaking and re-forming chemical bonds. Pasteur started with a 50 : 50 mixture of the two chiral tartaric acid enantiomers, a racemate.

prompt: What does it mean to resolve a racemate?

choices.text: To separate it into its (+) and (−) enantiomers
To convert one enantiomer into the other until the mixture is 50 : 50
choices.why: That would make a racemate, not resolve one. Resolution separates the two enantiomers already present.

choices.text: To convert it into the meso compound
choices.why: A meso compound is a different compound; getting one from the enantiomers would require breaking and re-forming bonds.

choices.text: To measure its specific rotation
choices.why: A racemate shows no rotation. Resolving it means separating the enantiomers, each of which is optically active.

explanation: Through good luck, Pasteur was able to separate, or resolve, racemic tartaric acid into its (+) and (−) enantiomers.

prompt: Why aren't most racemates resolved the way Pasteur resolved tartaric acid?

choices.text: The fractional crystallization technique he used doesn't work for most racemates
His technique destroys one of the two enantiomers
choices.why: Pasteur obtained both the (+) and (−) forms. The limitation is that fractional crystallization doesn't separate most racemates.

choices.text: Most racemates are really meso compounds
choices.why: A racemate is a mixture of two chiral enantiomers; a meso compound is a single achiral compound.

choices.text: Most racemates already rotate plane-polarized light, so they need no resolution
choices.why: Racemates show no optical rotation, because the rotations of the two enantiomers cancel.

explanation: Through good luck, Pasteur was able to separate racemic tartaric acid into its (+) and (−) enantiomers. Unfortunately, the fractional crystallization technique he used doesn't work for most racemates, so other methods are needed.

prompt: What is the most common method for resolving the racemate of a chiral carboxylic acid, RCO2H?

choices.text: React it with a single enantiomer of a chiral amine to form diastereomeric ammonium salts, then separate the salts
React it with an achiral amine such as methylamine, then separate the ammonium salts
choices.why: An achiral amine gives a racemic mixture of enantiomeric salts, which are no easier to separate than the acids.

choices.text: Crystallize it fractionally, as Pasteur did
choices.why: Fractional crystallization worked for tartaric acid through good luck but doesn't work for most racemates.

choices.text: Heat it until one enantiomer converts into the meso form
choices.why: Enantiomers can't become a different compound without breaking and re-forming bonds, and many acids have no meso form.

explanation: The most common method is an acid-base reaction between the acid and an amine base (RNH2) to yield an ammonium salt. When the amine is a single enantiomer, such as (R)-1-phenylethylamine, the products are diastereomers, which have different properties and can be separated (Figure 5.8.2).

prompt: Racemic lactic acid reacts with methylamine, CH3NH2, an achiral amine. What is the product?

choices.text: A racemic mixture of two enantiomeric salts, methylammonium (+)-lactate and methylammonium (−)-lactate
Two diastereomeric salts that can be separated by crystallization
choices.why: Diastereomers form only when the amine is chiral. With achiral methylamine, the two salts are mirror images.

choices.text: A single salt, because methylamine reacts with only one enantiomer
choices.why: Both (+)- and (−)-lactic acid react with methylamine equally well, just as left and right hands pick up a ball equally well.

choices.text: An achiral meso salt
choices.why: Each salt keeps the chirality center of its lactic acid, so the products are chiral enantiomers, not a meso compound.

explanation: Like left and right hands picking up an achiral ball, both (+)- and (−)-lactic acid react with methylamine equally well, and the product is a racemic mixture of the two enantiomers methylammonium (+)-lactate and methylammonium (−)-lactate (Figure 5.8.1).

prompt: Racemic lactic acid reacts with (R)-1-phenylethylamine. Which salts form?

choices.text: The R,R salt and the S,R salt, which are diastereomers
The R,R salt and the S,S salt, which are enantiomers
choices.why: Only the R amine is present, so every salt contains R amine. An S,S salt would need (S)-1-phenylethylamine.

choices.text: Only the R,R salt, because the R amine reacts only with (R)-lactic acid
choices.why: Both enantiomers of lactic acid react with the amine, but they give different products.

choices.text: The R,R salt and the S,R salt, which are enantiomers
choices.why: R,R and S,R differ at only one chirality center, so they aren't mirror images; they are diastereomers.

explanation: (R)-Lactic acid reacts with (R)-1-phenylethylamine to give the R,R salt, and (S)-lactic acid reacts with the R amine to give the S,R salt. The two salts are diastereomers, not enantiomers (Figure 5.8.2).

prompt: Why can the salts from racemic lactic acid and (R)-1-phenylethylamine be separated, when the salts from racemic lactic acid and methylamine cannot?

choices.text: The (R)-amine gives diastereomers, which have different chemical and physical properties
The (R)-amine reacts with only one enantiomer of lactic acid, leaving the other unreacted
choices.why: Both enantiomers react with the chiral amine; they simply give two different (diastereomeric) salts.

choices.text: The (R)-amine gives enantiomers, and enantiomers have different melting points
choices.why: Enantiomers have identical physical properties apart from the sign of their rotation. The methylamine salts are enantiomers, which is why they can't be separated easily.

choices.text: 1-Phenylethylamine is a stronger base than methylamine
choices.why: Base strength isn't the point. What matters is that the amine is a single enantiomer of a chiral compound.

explanation: With a single enantiomer of a chiral amine, the two salts are diastereomers, not enantiomers. They have different chemical and physical properties, and it may therefore be possible to separate them by crystallization or some other means. Achiral methylamine gives a racemic mixture of enantiomeric salts.

prompt: The book compares the reaction of racemic lactic acid with (R)-1-phenylethylamine to left and right hands putting on a right-handed glove. What does the glove represent?

choices.text: The single enantiomer of the chiral amine
Achiral methylamine
choices.why: Methylamine is the ball in the other analogy: achiral, and picked up equally well by both hands.

choices.text: The racemic lactic acid
choices.why: The left and right hands are the two lactic acid enantiomers.

choices.text: The strong acid used to recover the lactic acid
choices.why: The glove is the chiral reagent that the two enantiomers combine with. Right hand in right glove and left hand in right glove are similar but different, like diastereomers.

explanation: Left and right hands (the lactic acid enantiomers) don't put on a right-handed glove (a single enantiomer of a chiral amine) in the same way, so the products are not mirror images; they're similar but different, just as the R,R and S,R salts are diastereomers.

prompt: After the two diastereomeric salts of lactic acid and (R)-1-phenylethylamine have been separated, how are the pure lactic acid enantiomers obtained?

choices.text: By acidifying each salt with a strong acid, which also lets the chiral amine be recovered for reuse
By adding methylamine to each salt
choices.why: Adding another base doesn't free the carboxylic acid. Acidification with a strong acid gives back the acid and the protonated amine.

choices.text: No further step is needed; the salts are the pure enantiomers of lactic acid
choices.why: Each salt still contains the amine. It has to be acidified to release the free lactic acid.

choices.text: By mixing the two salts back together and crystallizing
choices.why: Mixing them would undo the separation. Each separated salt is acidified on its own.

explanation: Once separated, acidification of the two diastereomeric salts with a strong acid makes it possible to isolate the two pure enantiomers of lactic acid and to recover the chiral amine for reuse.

prompt: Racemic 2-phenylpropanoic acid, CH3CH(C6H5)CO2H, is treated with (S)-1-phenylethylamine. How many different (diastereomeric) ammonium salts form?
explanation: The (R)-acid gives the R,S salt and the (S)-acid gives the S,S salt. The two salts are diastereomers with different properties, so they can be separated, as in the resolution of lactic acid (Figure 5.8.2).

prompt: Racemic (±)-2-methylbutanoic acid, CH3CH2CH(CH3)CO2H, reacts with ethanol, an achiral alcohol, to form an ester. What is the product?

choices.text: A racemic mixture of the (R) and (S) esters, which are enantiomers
A mixture of two diastereomeric esters
choices.why: Diastereomers would need a chiral partner. Ethanol is achiral, so the two products are mirror images.

choices.text: A single ester enantiomer, because ethanol reacts with only one enantiomer
choices.why: An achiral reagent reacts with both enantiomers equally well, like a ball picked up by either hand.

choices.text: An achiral ester, because the ethanol cancels the chirality
choices.why: The chirality center of the acid is unchanged, so each ester is chiral; together they form a racemate.

explanation: Reaction of a racemic acid with an achiral alcohol yields a racemic mixture of mirror-image (enantiomeric) products (compare Worked Example 5.8.1). A chiral partner is needed to give diastereomers.
